case_info.scenario: A 61-year-old man presented to our clinic with a 3-month history of rapidly growing and itchy cutaneous nodules all over the body. He denied systemic complaints such as weakness, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Oral glucocorticoids did not show any therapeutic effect. His medical history was remarkable for mild anemia because of untreated hemorrhoids. Physical examination revealed numerous symmetrically distributed, well-defined, erythematous skin nodules on his back, buttocks, and limb extensors (Figure, A). Prominent lymphadenopathies on bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes were noted, with the largest lymph node measuring approximately 5 × 2 cm. Laboratory tests were significant for atypical lymphocytes in the peripheral blood (count up to 6%), an elevated CD4+/CD8+lymphocyte ratio (9.21; normal range, 0.7-3.1), moderate anemia (hemoglobin level, 8.7 g/dL; normal range, 11.5-15.0 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0]), a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (35 mm/h; normal range, 0-25 mm/h), and cryoglobulins composed of mixed polyclonal immunoglobulins. The platelet count (161 × 103/μL; normal range, 125-350 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 1.0]) and lactate dehydrogenase (217 U/L; normal range, 100-240 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]) were normal. Quantification of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA showed high loads of virus in the peripheral blood (846 copies/mL in serum, 27 700 copies/mL in lymphocytes; normal range, <500 copies/mL). A biopsy specimen from a skin nodule was sent for histopathologic examination (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Physical examination showed widespread, symmetrically distributed, well-defined nodules on the trunk and extremities. B, Skin biopsy sample showed infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes with proliferation of high endothelial venules (hematoxylin-eosin). C, In situ hybridization was positive for Epstein-Barr virus in the skin.
case_info.explanation: D. Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an

case_info.caption: A, Physical examination showed widespread, symmetrically distributed, well-defined nodules on the trunk and extremities. B, Skin biopsy sample showed infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes with proliferation of high endothelial venules (hematoxylin-eosin). C, In situ hybridization was positive for Epstein-Barr virus in the skin.
case_info.explanation: D. Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

[Core Objective]

case_info.explanation: D. Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:

A 61-year-old man presented to our clinic with a 3-month history of rapidly growing and itchy cutaneous nodules all over the body. He denied systemic complaints such as weakness, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Oral glucocorticoids did not show any therapeutic effect. His medical history was remarkable for mild anemia because of untreated hemorrhoids. Physical examination revealed numerous symmetrically distributed, well-defined, erythematous skin nodules on his back, buttocks, and limb extensors (Figure, A). Prominent lymphadenopathies on bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes were noted, with the largest lymph node measuring approximately 5 × 2 cm. Laboratory tests were significant for atypical lymphocytes in the peripheral blood (count up to 6%), an elevated CD4+/CD8+lymphocyte ratio (9.21; normal range, 0.7-3.1), moderate anemia (hemoglobin level, 8.7 g/dL; normal range, 11.5-15.0 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0]), a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (35 mm/h; normal range, 0-25 mm/h), and cryoglobulins composed of mixed polyclonal immunoglobulins. Quantification of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA showed high loads of virus in the peripheral blood (846 copies/mL in serum, 27 700 copies/mL in lymphocytes; normal range, <500 copies/mL). A biopsy specimen from a skin nodule was sent for histopathologic examination (Figure, B).

case_info.explanation: D. Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.

   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

case_info.explanation: D. Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

case_info.explanation: D. Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

1. Mental Demand

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.

       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.

case_info.scenario: A 61-year-old man presented to our clinic with a 3-month history of rapidly growing and itchy cutaneous nodules all over the body. He denied systemic complaints such as weakness, fever, night sweats, or weight loss. Oral glucocorticoids did not show any therapeutic effect. His medical history was remarkable for mild anemia because of untreated hemorrhoids. Physical examination revealed numerous symmetrically distributed, well-defined, erythematous skin nodules on his back, buttocks, and limb extensors (Figure, A). Prominent lymphadenopathies on bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes were noted, with the largest lymph node measuring approximately 5 × 2 cm. Laboratory tests were significant for atypical lymphocytes in the peripheral blood (count up to 6%), an elevated CD4+/CD8+lymphocyte ratio (9.21; normal range, 0.7-3.1), moderate anemia (hemoglobin level, 8.7 g/dL; normal range, 11.5-15.0 g/dL [to convert to g/L, multiply by 10.0]), a high erythrocyte sedimentation rate (35 mm/h; normal range, 0-25 mm/h), and cryoglobulins composed of mixed polyclonal immunoglobulins. The platelet count (161 × 103/μL; normal range, 125-350 × 103/μL [to convert to ×109/L, multiply by 1.0]) and lactate dehydrogenase (217 U/L; normal range, 100-240 U/L [to convert to μkat/L, multiply by 0.0167]) were normal. Quantification of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA showed high loads of virus in the peripheral blood (846 copies/mL in serum, 27 700 copies/mL in lymphocytes; normal range, <500 copies/mL). A biopsy specimen from a skin nodule was sent for histopathologic examination (Figure, B).
case_info.caption: A, Physical examination showed widespread, symmetrically distributed, well-defined nodules on the trunk and extremities. B, Skin biopsy sample showed infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes with proliferation of high endothelial venules (hematoxylin-eosin). C, In situ hybridization was positive for Epstein-Barr virus in the skin.
case_info.explanation: D. Cutaneous angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma The skin biopsy displayed diffuse infiltration of atypical lymphocytes and histiocytes in the dermis and subcutis, with proliferation of high endothelial venules (HEVs). The lymphocytes stained positively for CD3, CD4, CD8, BCL6, and PD1 and were negative for CD20, CD30, or CD56, indicating a T follicular helper (TFH) phenotype. The Ki-67 labeling index was 40%. In situ hybridization for EBV-encoded RNA (EBER) demonstrated scattered positivity (Figure, C). A positron emission tomography–computed tomography scan showed increased glucose accumulation on the skin nodules (standardized uptake value, 7.7) and multiple lymph nodes (standardized uptake value, 1.7-4.9). The lymph node biopsy showed total effacement of nodal architecture, diffuse infiltration of medium-sized lymphocytes with pale cytoplasm in a polymorphous inflammatory background containing plasma cells and eosinophils, and marked proliferation of HEVs. The immunostaining revealed a TFH phenotype and expanded follicular dendritic cell (FDC) meshwork. Monoclonal rearrangements of T-cell receptor genes and positive EBER were also revealed. Then, the diagnosis of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma (AITL) was made. Genetic profiling identified hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation,DNMT3AG543Asequence variation, and 2TET2frameshift sequence variations (Q1526fs and E1728fs) in both skin and lymph node tissues. Bone marrow biopsy showed no lymphoma involvement. The patient received chemotherapy and achieved complete remission after 6 cycles of CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). His skin nodules subsided remarkably after the first cycle. Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a common aggressive form of peripheral T-cell lymphoma arising from CD4+TFH cells.1Patients typically present with the acute onset of a systemic illness (fever, weight loss, and/or night sweats) and generalized lymphadenopathy. The lymph node biopsy demonstrates a polymorphous infiltrate including atypical lymphocytes that are positive for TFH cell markers and a prominent proliferation of HEVs and FDCs. Epstein-Barr virus infections are present in 66% to 91% of patients with AITL.2Epstein-Barr virus–positive B immunoblasts are detected by in situ hybridizations for small nuclear EBERs in areas between FDCs. Sequence variations inTET2,RHOA,DNMT3A, andIDH2are recurrent in AITL. The hotspotRHOAG17Vsequence variation occurs in 50% to 70% of patients with AITL.2 Skin manifestations occur in up to 50% of patients with AITL. These lesions can be categorized as nonspecific macular or papular eruptions mimicking drug/viral exanthemas and plaque-like or nodular lesions that are more likely to be recognized as lymphomatous.3The histopathology of cutaneous AITL is not specific, usually presenting as nodular or perivascular infiltration of lymphocytes with or without cytological atypia.4,5The positive rates of BCL6, CXCL13, and PD-1 in the skin lesion reach up to 43%, 62%, and 81%, respectively.5Other extranodal involvement, including hepatomegaly and splenomegaly, frequently presents in AITL. Immune system–mediated abnormalities are common in AITL and can include elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate, hemolytic anemia, cryoglobulins, and polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia. There is no standardized treatment for AITL, and CHOP is the initial regimen in most cases. Although spontaneous remissions occasionally happen, AITL is an aggressive disorder with a 5-year survival of 32% to 41%.6 Cutaneous sarcoidosis often presents as red-brown to violaceous papules and plaques. It is histologically characterized by noncaseating epithelioid granulomas and usually responds to steroids.7Blastic plasmacytoid dendritic cell neoplasm generally manifests as cutaneous nodules and bruise-like patches. Neoplastic cells infiltrate into the dermis and fat lobules with the expression of plasmacytoid dendritic cell–associated antigens.8,9Lymphomatoid granulomatosis is universally extranodal. It is an EBV-driven B-cell lymphoproliferative disorder and can be ruled out by histologic characteristics.10 Because the clinical symptoms and histopathological results in cutaneous AITL are nonspecific, the diagnosis is frequently delayed or missed. The quickly progressive skin lesions, multiple immunological abnormalities, generalized lymphadenopathy, and aberrant lymphocytic infiltration with TFH markers and EBER helped to coin the diagnosis of AITL. Recognizing the extranodal symptoms and signs is pivotal to the early intervention of this rapidly progressive disease.

You are a deliberation POLICY steering a conversation between a medical AI and a clinician toward
the best decision, at the lowest cognitive cost to the clinician. You control HOW the AI speaks,
never WHAT the medical answer is (that is the AI's job). Each turn you choose ONE control stage and

The 3 control stages (pick exactly one, and only from the reachable list you are given):

- EXPAND  — cheap, safe, broadens the picture. Elicit the clinician's reasoning, ask them to
            justify, or surface a missing goal/criterion/perspective. Do NOT yet evaluate or push
            an option. Effect is often delayed (sets up a later CHALLENGE). Use when the state is
            unclear or the clinician hasn't exposed their rationale.
- CHALLENGE — expensive and highest-yield, but also most likely to make the clinician regress.
            Directly evaluate the option on the table against a goal/criterion, or contrast two
            options, and press the clinician to engage the mismatch. Spend it deliberately: when
            you have reason to think the clinician's current position is wrong or under-examined.
- CONVERGE — cheap, terminal. Recommend the now-best-supported option and invite accept/reject,
            or confirm an agreement already reached. This is the STOP / pacing lever — stop
            spending burden once belief has settled.

{{
  "stage": "EXPAND | CHALLENGE | CONVERGE",
  "reason": "one short sentence: the hidden state you infer and why this stage now",
  "action_guidance": "concrete HOW-instruction for the AI's next utterance (no option letter/answer)"
}}

Physical examination revealed numerous symmetrically distributed, well-defined, erythematous skin nodules on his back, buttocks, and limb extensors (Figure, A). Prominent lymphadenopathies on bilateral cervical, axillary, and inguinal lymph nodes were noted, with the largest lymph node measuring approximately 5 × 2 cm. Quantification of Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) DNA showed high loads of virus in the peripheral blood (846 copies/mL in serum, 27 700 copies/mL in lymphocytes; normal range, <500 copies/mL).
